messages.subject: Mesh Clarification
parts:
Hello all,

I am predicting water quality in a bay area and have a question about using a stationary or barrier model.  I recently made the switch from space-time kriging in gstat because I want to produce more accurate predictions in the tributaries of my study area.  I was thinking about non-Euclidean kriging, but INLA seems much better for what I need. Please see the attachments for my study area, sample points, and mesh.

I am seeing that the barrier model is slightly better than the stationary model; but the RMSE and other validation stats suggest that I can use a stationary model for my example.  I expected the barrier model to perform much better because it enforces that there is land between the tributaries.  Just need some clarification:

In general, when adding my study area's polygon to create the mesh, does this already address the notion of "water distances/non-Euclidean distance"? In other words, the distances between the sample points follow a path within the polygon, not outside of it.

Thanks for your time,

Michael

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Mesh Clarification
parts:
Hi Michael,

I am not entirely sure what you mean, but I will try.

When you specify the barrier.triangles, then
"this already address the notion of "water distances/non-Euclidean distance""

as you say.
But the mesh itself does not.

Can you plot the barrier polygon for me? 
?INLA::inla.barrier.polygon

For prediction, spatial non-stationarity is a lot about covariance, which means that the RMSE in-sample or for small holdouts might be very similar to a stationary model. But: Try to hold out all the points in a group on one side of land, and check the out of sample RMSE for predicting those.

Best regards,
Haakon Bakka
